list.listitem: The diagnosis of hydatidiform mole (HM) should be considered if a patient presents with first trimester bleeding and/or any of the following findings: previous molar pregnancy, hyperemesis, uterine size greater than dates, gestational hypertension, or signs of thyrotoxicosis. C

Placental abnormalities seen on ultrasound combined with quantitative beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (b-HCG) levels support the diagnosis of HM and histology confirms. Ultrasound. however, may miss up to 2/3rds of cases of partial HM.C
Complete and partial HMs are treated with surgical evacuation. C

After surgical treatment, molar pregnancies should be followed with serial quantitative b-HCG levels every 1 to 2 weeks until three consecutive normal assays, then twice (benign HM) or monthly (non-invasive gestational trophoblastic neoplasm) for 6 months. C
The diagnosis of postmolar gestational trophoblastic disease can be made if serum b-HCG levels plateau, rise, or are still present at 6 months. C

background.definition: Hydatidiform mole (HM) is a benign type of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD); the benign forms include complete HM and partial HM. These tumors, both benign and malignant, develop in the uterus from placental tissue. HM involves proliferation and edema of the chorionic villi and carries the risk of subsequent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). HM is the most common form of GTD accounting for 80% of these tumors followed by invasive mole (15%). In addition to invasive hydatidiform mole, GTNs include choriocarcinoma, placental-site trophoblastic tumor and epithelioid trophoblastic tumor.

list.listitem: In North America and Europe 0.5 to 1.0 per 1000 pregnancies.
In a study of 26,101 consecutive miscarriages, molar pregnancy was detected in 3.1% with the use of 24-chromosome SNP microarray testing; most were partial HM (2.8%).
In Denmark the diagnosis of HM decreased from 2.55/1000 in 1999 to 1.6/1000 in 2014. The authors speculate this decrease may be related to decreased histopathologic review of products of conception.
In the Netherlands, the overall incidence rate was 1.67 per 1000 deliveries per year, a rate that has stabilized over the past decade.
The incidence increased in England and Wales from 1:611 viable conceptions to 1:528 in 2008; the highest-risk group were women older than 49 years (17%).
Higher rates have been reported in Asia.

In a single-institution retrospective study of 25,667 fresh embryo transfer ICSI procedures out of 41,540 ICSI cycles over 8 years, the frequency of gestational trophoblastic disease was calculated 10 cases in 41,540 (0.240 per 1000) ICSI procedures and 10 in 25,667 (0.389 per 1000) fresh embryo transfers following ICSI cycles. Ten cases occurred in 8,196 (1.220 per 1000) clinical pregnancies.
The incidence of choriocarcinoma is reported as 1 per 40,000 pregnancies in North America and Europe, 9.2 per 40,000 pregnancies in Southeast Asia and 3.3 per 40 000 pregnancies in Japan.

Prior history of a HM is a risk factor for subsequent GTN; malignancy is 2 to 3 times more likely to occur with a complete HM compared to a partial HM (8%-15% vs 1%-6%). Authors of a recent meta-analysis of 19 studies found an incidence of GTN following complete mole of 15.7% (1,354/8,611, 95% CI 15.0-16.5%) and 3.95% following partial mole (221/5,593, 95% CI 3.47-4.50%).

There is an association between GTD and hyperthyroidism. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) can stimulate the thyroid causing thyrotoxicosis. In a study of 50 women with HM, 17 (34%) required preoperative anti-thyroid treatment. Hyperthyroidism was associated with hCG levels - a TSH <0.2 IU/L was found in 17/30 women with hCG levels >200,000 uIU/L and 15/20 women with hCG levels >400,000 uIU/L. The 15 women with complete HM had lower TSH level and higher fT4 and TT4 levels than the 35 women with partial HM.
About 50% of GTN follows molar pregnancy.
HM results from abnormal fertilization, precise mechanism is unknown.

Complete HMs arise from fertilization of an ovum lacking nuclear DNA and have either two identical paternal chromosome complements from duplication of the haploid genome of a single sperm (80%) or from fertilization by two sperms resulting in diploid or tetraploid karyotype. Partial HM occur when an ovum retains its nucleus and abnormal fertilization occurs similarly by duplication of the haploid genome of a single sperm or from fertilization by two sperms resulting in triploid karyotype.
In rare cases of familial recurrent molar pregnancy, complete HM has a bi-parental chromosomal pattern and is associated with a mutation in the genes NLRP7 or KHDC3L.

A recent retrospective review in South Korea found that cesarean delivery was a strong risk factor for post molar GTN and invasive mole. Women who had a cesarean delivery had a 5-fold increased risk for post molar GTN.

The incidence of HM is positively correlated with the per capita intake of rice, fish, shrimp, and animal fat; and negatively correlated with the per capita intake of wheat flour, starch and sugar, protein, and iron.
The use of oral contraceptives following the diagnosis of molar pregnancy does not increase the likelihood of progression to malignant trophoblastic disease.
HM is classified into complete and partial.

Histologically, choriocarcinoma is characterized by abnormal intermediate trophoblast and cytotrophoblast, rimmed with syncytiotrophoblasts with areas of necrosis and hemorrhage. Choriocarcinoma can be found in tubes, ovaries, lung, liver, spleen, kidneys, bowel, or brain.

Using a histopathologic comparison between complete HMs and first trimester placentas, 3,729 of 14,022 protein-coding genes expressed in both samples, including placenta-specific, imprinted and immune genes, were differentially expressed in complete HMs. "Cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction" was the most impacted of 38 dysregulated pathways. Complex dysregulation was observed with down-regulated placental functions, altered imprinted gene expression, and activated immune pathways.
See .

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Younger (<20 years) or older (>35 years) maternal age

list.listitem: Consider prophylactic chemotherapy (methotrexate or dactinomycin) in women with a complete HM who are at high risk of post-molar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guideline on GTN (2019) identifies high risk as: women who are >age 40 years, have hCG levels in excess of 100,000 mIU/mL, excessive uterine enlargement (>20 weeks) and/or theca lutein cysts >6 cm.

Authors of a Cochrane review of three low-quality RCTs with 550 participants with complete molar pregnancies found reduced risk of subsequent GTN (RR 0.37, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.24-0.57) with prophylactic chemotherapy. However, the authors were unable to recommend this practice based on poor study methodological quality, small sizes of the included studies, and considering the risks of prophylactic chemotherapy including possible increased drug resistance, delays in treatment of GTN, toxic side effects.

The Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SGOC, 2021) recommend prophylactic chemotherapy be considered only for high-risk patients who are unlikely to return for regular follow up, based on very low-level evidence.

The diagnosis of HM should be considered if a patient presents with first trimester bleeding and/or any of the following findings: uterine size greater than dates, hyperemesis, gestational hypertension/preeclampsia, or signs of thyrotoxicosis. C
Placental abnormalities seen on ultrasound combined with quantitative b-hCG levels confirm the diagnosis of hydatidiform mole. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Absence of fetal cardiac activity with normal placenta
Presence of hematoma on ultrasound with a viable fetus

list.listitem: Patients with molar pregnancies usually present with first or early second trimester bleeding. In one case series of 74 women with complete HM, bleeding occurred in 84%. Other signs and symptoms were less common and included uterine size greater than dates (28%), hyperemesis (8%), and gestational hypertension/preeclampsia (1.3%). None of these women had signs of thyrotoxicosis compared to 7% noted in prior studies.
Women with partial HM are often (15% to 60%) misdiagnosed as having incomplete or missed abortions because of the presence of fetal or embryonic tissue and amniotic fluid.
Fetal heart tones are absent.

If symptoms of pregnancy persist 4 to 6 weeks after termination of pregnancy, evacuation of a non-viable pregnancy or spontaneous abortion, a serum or urine b-hCG test may allow earlier diagnosis of GTD when products of conception are not routinely sent for pathology.

A quantitative b-hCG and pelvic ultrasound should be obtained. Approximately half of women with complete HMs have an hCG >100,000 mIU/mL compared with only 10% of patients with partial HM, which grows more slowly.

The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) 2000 criteria used for the diagnosis of postmolar GTN includes a rise in b-hCG for three consecutive weekly measurements over at least a period of 2 weeks or more (on days 1, 7, 14) OR when the plateau of hCG lasts for four measurements over a period of 3 weeks or longer (on days 1, 7, 14, 21) OR if there is histologically-confirmed choriocarcinoma.

Ultrasound findings are typically described as an echogenic pattern of villous edema and intrauterine blood clots instead of normal placental tissue. These findings are diffuse with complete and more focal with partial molar pregnancy. Pelvic ultrasound has a sensitivity of 70% to 90% and specificity of 74% for diagnosing a complete HM.
Diagnosis of partial HM is lower than complete HM as up to 2/3rds may be missed on ultrasound.

Authors of a meta-analysis and narrative synthesis of 8 studies of ultrasound found a sensitivity of ultrasound for diagnosing HM of 52.2% and specificity of 92.6%, making it more useful when positive than negative (LR+ 6.9, LR- 0.5). Both sensitivity and specificity were lower for partial vs. complete mole (sensitivity 32.1% vs. 81.5%, respectively) and rates of misdiagnosis were about 38%. Findings are operator dependent and sensitivity appears higher with more advanced gestational age.
The diagnosis of HM is confirmed on histopathologic testing of uterine contents.

If a molar pregnancy is suspected based on these tests, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guideline on Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia (2019) recommends obtaining a CBC with platelets (anemia); liver, renal, and thyroid function tests (preeclampsia, hyperthyroidism); chemistry profile (electrolyte abnormality if hyperemesis), blood type and screen (administration of rhoD immune globulin if Rh negative).

Recommended imaging includes a chest X-ray (metastases, if GTN). To complete a metastatic workup, NCCN recommends chest/abdominal/pelvic CT scan with contrast (or MRI if contrast is contraindicated) and brain MRI (preferred) or brain CT if pulmonary metastasis.

Molecular genotyping can aid in the diagnosis of partial HM, if histopathologic criteria are not definitive or in cases of familial complete HM. Compared to genotyping to diagnose complete HM, p57KIP2 immunostaining was highly accurate with an area under the curve of (AUC) 0.980.

Consider genotype testing for fetal triploidy in products of conception because the diagnosis of first trimester partial HM can be difficult and there is a high prevalence of partial HM among products of conception with fetal triploidy. In one study of 20 specimens of products of conception with fetal triploidy, 65% (13) were partial HM, and 4 of those 13 were initially interpreted as normal or non-molar with minimal abnormalities on histopathology.
See algorithm in for an overview of management.

In a patient presenting with first trimester bleeding, consider molar pregnancy in women with previous molar pregnancy, uterine size greater than dates, hyperemesis, gestational hypertension, or signs of thyrotoxicosis.

Order quantitative b-HCG and pelvic ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis and look for other causes of symptoms. The early diagnosis of molar pregnancies may not always be identified by ultrasound alone.

Complete and partial HMs are treated with surgical evacuation – suction dilation and curettage, preferably under ultrasound guidance. Hysterectomy is considered for older women who do not wish to preserve fertility. C

Choriocarcinoma and invasive HM are treated with chemotherapy; single chemotherapeutic agents are effective for low-risk tumors and high-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasms (GTNs) are treated with multiple agents. C
All Rh-negative women should be offered anti-D immune globulin at uterine evacuation to prevent alloimmunization.

Post-molar GTN is diagnosed based on hCG surveillance. Treatment (chemotherapy) is based on risk scoring using the modified World Health Organization scoring system adapted by FIGO (Fédération Internationale de Gynécologie et d’Obstétrique) and FIGO staging. Risk scoring is based on eight factors: age, antecedent pregnancy, interval from index pregnancy, pretreatment serum hCG, largest tumor size, site of metastases, number of metastases, and previous failed chemotherapy. Low risk GTN is <7 on the prognostic score. The scoring system can be viewed at https://www.cancer.net/cancer-types/gestational-trophoblastic-disease/stage-and-risk-grouping.

Treatment algorithms are provided in the NCCN gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (2019) guideline. Women with low-risk GTN are treated with single agent (methotrexate or dactinomycin) chemotherapy and women with high-risk GTN (defined as FIGO stages II-III disease with a prognostic score ≥7 or FIGO stage IV disease and comprising about 6% of patients) are most often treated with EMA/CO (etoposide, methotrexate, and dactinomycin alternating with cyclophosphamide and vincristine) or EMA/CP (etoposide, methotrexate, actinomycin-D, etoposide, and cisplatin).

Authors of a Cochrane review of seven randomized clinical trials with 667 patients with low-risk GTN concluded that dactinomycin (actinomycin D) was associated with significantly higher primary cure rates than methotrexate (RR 0.65; 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.57-0.75) and fewer treatment failures. Side effects were not consistently reported but side effects associated with pulsed dactinomycin appear comparable to low-dose methotrexate.

Authors of a Cochrane review of a single trial found combination methotrexate, actinomycin D and chlorambucil as effective as but less toxic than combination cyclophosphamide, hydroxyurea, actinomycin D, methotrexate, doxorubicin, melphalan and vincristine.

Choriocarcinoma and invasive HM respond well to chemotherapy. The other types of GTNs (choriocarcinoma, placental-site trophoblastic tumor and epithelioid trophoblastic tumor) are rare and not covered in this chapter (see NCCN guideline).

For high-risk GTN, authors of one review concluded that modern preferred chemotherapy (EMA/CO or EMA/CP) was associated with lower mortality (overall: 8.8% vs 9.5%; comparative meta-analysis: 8.1% vs 12.4%; OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.20-0.90, 14 studies).
All diagnosed molar pregnancies should be surgically evacuated by dilation and curettage (D&C). Alternatively, patients can be considered for hysterectomy.

Hysterectomy among those 40 years and older was found to be more protective for subsequent GTN than uterine evacuation, with an OR of 0.19 (95% CI 0.08-0.48), based on a systematic literature review and meta-analysis.

A second D&C alone can be considered for women whose pathology indicates non-invasive GTN. In one study of 64 women with newly diagnosed low-risk, nonmetastatic GTN, 24 (40%) experienced a cure without need for chemotherapy. Risk factors for failed surgical treatment were age <20 years or >39 years.
In another RCT of 89 women with low-risk GTN, second uterine curettage did not reduce the number of chemotherapy courses required to reach normalization of hCG or affect relapse rate.

Twin pregnancy with a complete HM and co-existing viable fetus is rare. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found 72 cases from 6 case series with an average duration of pregnancy of 34 weeks (range 25-41 weeks) and an average rate of live birth of 34.4%. Most (72.2%) were delivered via cesarean section and 20 cases (27.8%) had vaginal deliveries.
GTN is relatively rare and can be fatal. Therefore, patients should be co-managed with a specialist with experience in management of this condition.

The SOCG (2021) recommends that women diagnosed with GTN should promptly be referred to a gynecologic oncologist for staging, risk scoring and treatment. They also recommend that women who become pregnant during the follow up period for GTD or GTN be referred to a gynecologic oncologist and Maternal Fetal Medicine specialist for assessment and management.

listitem.strong: Persistent or recurrent gestational trophoblastic disease

list.listitem: In an Australian database study, risk of developing persistent disease in women with partial or complete molar pregnancy was 11.3% (78/686). Risk was increased if b-hCG failed to reach negative by 12 weeks postevacuation and risk markedly decreased if the time from the last pregnancy was more than 12 months.

Risk of recurrent mole is 1 in 100 for women with a complete HM but only minimally increased for women following a partial hydatidiform mole. For women with one or two consecutive complete molar pregnancies, there is a recurrence risk of between 10% and 25%.
Rates of GTN following a complete HM range from 15% to 28%.

In a retrospective study of 7761 patients in the French National Center for Trophoblastic Diseases database whose b-HCG levels returned spontaneously to normal, twenty (0.26%) developed GTN. No patients (0 of 2592 cases) with histologically-proven partial mole developed GTN compared to 0.36% for complete mole (18 of 5045) and 2.1% (2 of 95) for twin molar pregnancy. Risk factors associated with developing GTN after the end of the normal b-HCG monitoring period were age of ≥45 years (OR 8.3, 95% CI 2.0-32.7) and time to HCG normalization of ≥8 weeks (OR 7.7, 95% CI 1.1-335).
Earlier detection of complete hydatidiform mole (9 weeks vs. 12 weeks) does not appear to affect the risk of development of postmolar GTN.

In a registry study from New England of 1029 women with complete HM, women whose hCG level was below 50 mIU/mL during their follow-up were found to be at no more than 1.1% risk for developing persistent GTN while those with hCG levels above 2000 mIU/mL in the fourth week after evacuation (13.3% of women) had a 63.8% risk of developing persistent disease.

In a follow-up study of 1088 patients with GTD in Senegal, 108 were diagnosed and treated for GTN including 88 low-risk and 20 high-risk. Low-risk patients received an average of 6.9 cycles of initial single-agent chemotherapy and 12 patients with persistent disease were switched to a second-line multi-agent chemotherapy; nearly all (94.3%) achieved remission, but 5 patients subsequently died of their disease. All high-risk patients were initially treated with multi-agent chemotherapy, averaging 7 cycles. Twelve of the 20 high-risk patients died of their disease with an average survival time of 9.9 months (95% CI, 5.369-14.429).

In one study, a caspase-3 apoptotic index <4% was a strong risk factor for subsequent GTN with an OR of 35.5 (95% CI 14.0-90.1; P) in the derivation cohort and OR 25.7 (95% CI 10.1-65.3) in the validation cohort, a positive predictive value of 49% and 41%, respectively, and a negative predictive value of 97% in both cohorts.

A FIGO prognostic score of ≥7 is used to predict resistance to single-agent chemotherapy in patients with GTN. In a French database study of 974 patients, the 5-year mortality rate was 2% (95% CI 1.25%-3.13%) for all women, 12% among women with a FIGO score ≥7, and 38.4% (95% CI 23.4%-58.6%) among women with a FIGO score ≥13.

In a follow-up database study of 196 women with FIGO high-risk GTN in England, overall survival was 94%, with a median follow-up of 4.69 years; two women died within 4 weeks of starting treatment, 12 (6%) relapsed, and 9 patients subsequently died due to drug resistance.
Patients with a multiple gestation including a complete mole and a normally developing fetus had a high rate of spontaneous miscarriage and neonatal death in a 2024 retrospective cohort.

Subsequent reproductive outcomes in patients with complete and partial molar pregnancies and GTN remain similar to those in the general population with the exception of a slightly higher rate of stillbirth (1.3%) among women after successful chemotherapy for GTN.

Among women with complete HM and a coexistent normal fetus, authors of a meta-analysis of 14 studies with 244 cases found a high incidence of maternal complications (80.8% with vaginal bleeding, hyperthyroidism and/or pre-eclampsia) in ongoing pregnancies. There were 91 (50%) live births in ongoing pregnancies and 83 (34%) of the total cases were subsequently diagnosed with GTN.

Authors of a 2021 European meta-analysis of observational studies found that live birth after complete HM (53.6%) was statistically higher compared to live births after partial HM (51%). In addition, partial HM recurred more frequently after partial HM (0.4%) than complete HM (0.3%) and there was no significant difference in adverse obstetric outcomes between the two. No statistically significant difference was demonstrated for ectopic pregnancies, miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth, termination and complete molar recurrence after complete HM and partial HM pregnancies. These rates are similar to those in the general population.

For women following D&C for HM, NCCN recommends quantitative hCG assay monitoring every 1 to 2 weeks until levels have normalized, defined as 3 consecutive normal assays. In one database study, mean time to b-HCG remission was 12 weeks.

After initial normalization, hCG should be measured twice in 3-month intervals to ensure levels remain normal. In one large, retrospective case series, after a single normal hCG, the risk of GTN after a complete HM was 0.25% and after a partial HM was 0.03%. Authors of a meta-analysis if 19 studies found similar results with an incidence of GTN after normal hCG level of 64/18,357 (0.35%; 95% CI 0.27-0.45%) and partial mole of 5/14,864 (0.03%; 95% CI 0.01-0.08%). Most cases (89.6%) occurred when the time for the time from evacuation to hCG normalization was 56 days or longer.
For women following D&C for non-invasive post-molar GTN, NCCN recommends quantitative hCG assay monitoring every 2 weeks until 3 consecutive normal assays, then monthly for 6 months.

Laboratory monitoring is abnormal when one of the following 3 b-HCG criteria is documented: (1) failure of the b-hCG to continue to decline; documented by a plateau in the b-hCG levels over 3 weeks, (2) >10% increase in 3 values of b-hCG levels over a 2-week duration, or (3) detectable b-hCG levels 6 months after evacuation. B

A single reference lab should be used for follow-up hCG testing to minimize false-positive and false-negative tests. False positive tests can occur from the presence of heterophile antibodies or pituitary hCG, particularly in perimenopausal women; false negative tests sometimes occur with very high hCG levels.

Patients should be counseled to use reliable contraceptive methods during the monitoring process. Although data are limited, use of hormonal contraceptives appears safe and, in one study, did not affect time to b-HCG remission or development of GTN. IUDs can be considered once B-hCG levels are normalized (SOGC, 2020). Subsequent pregnancies should be monitored with an early ultrasound to confirm normal gestation and placenta. C

Although very rare, the possibility exists for a viable fetus to coexist with an HM. There are no clear guidelines on how to manage these patients and they should be counseled on both the increased risk of fetal complications (eg, abnormal karyotype, malformations) and maternal medical complications including metastatic disease.
In about one third of these cases, it is possible to have a live-born infant.

cell.label: History & Physical: hyperemesis, uterine size ≠ dates, gestational HTN, or signs of thyrotoxicosis?
Consider hydatidiform mole; obtain ultrasound. Ultrasound normal?
Placental abnormality consistent with molar pregnancy?
Consider partial mole vs. spontaneous abortion.
Continue work-up for other causes of first trimester bleeding.

feature.caption: Pathologic Features of Partial and Complete Hydatidiform Moles.
feature.feature_body:
Feature Partial Mole Complete Mole
Karyotype Usually 69,XXX or 69,XXY 46,XX or 46,XY
Embryo-fetus Often present Absent
Amnion, fetal red blood cells Often present Absent
Villous edema Variable, focal Diffuse
Trophoblastic proliferation Focal, slight to moderate Diffuse, slight to severe
Adapted from Gestational trophoblastic disease. Seils A, Edmonson KG, Davis K, eds. Williams Obstetrics. 22nd ed. New York, NY: McGraw Hill; 2005:274.
